Federal rules generally require an ATM to offer a receipt at the time you make a withdrawal, but there is an exception for small amounts. For transfers of $15 or less, the institution does not have to provide a receipt. Your $10 withdrawal falls under that exception, so the missing receipt is not a violation. You can still check the withdrawal in your account history or statement. If you see a withdrawal you did not make, contact the credit union right away.

Under federal funds-availability rules, cash you deposit in person with a teller must be made available for withdrawal no later than the first business day after the deposit. Since you deposited this morning, the funds should be available on the next business day. This is the general federal rule, and it does not cover every situation, so check with the credit union if you need the money sooner.

Cash deposited at an ATM is generally not covered by the next-business-day rule that applies to cash handed to a teller. Under Regulation CC, the next-day availability rule for cash applies to deposits made in person to an employee. An ATM deposit falls under the general availability rules for other deposits, so the money may take several business days to become available. The exact timing depends on the credit union's own funds availability policy, which must be disclosed to you. For an ordinary check deposited in person, the first $225 of the deposit must be available for withdrawal by the next business day after the deposit. The rest of the check amount may be held longer under the regulation's general schedule, which generally makes it available by the second business day after deposit. Certain exceptions can extend these holds, such as large deposits, redeposited checks, and accounts that have been open less than 30 days.

For a check drawn on a local bank, the credit union must make the first $225 of the deposit available for withdrawal no later than the next business day after the deposit. The rest of the check must be available no later than the second business day after the day you deposit it. Some exceptions apply, such as new accounts, very large deposits, and accounts with repeated overdrafts, which can allow the credit union to hold funds longer. Your account disclosures or a representative can tell you how these rules apply to your account.

If the funds have not appeared as expected, a representative can check the posting date and the credit union's policy on your account.

Under NCUA Part 707, a credit union generally must give you advance written notice before it makes a change to your account terms that could adversely affect you, such as a lower rate or yield, higher fees, or a changed term that reduces your benefit. The standard notice period is at least 30 days before the change takes effect. For a share certificate (a time account with a fixed maturity), the rules are stricter: the credit union generally cannot make an adverse change to the terms before maturity unless the account agreement disclosed that it reserved the right to do so. Your credit union must tell you, before you open the account, how dividends are calculated. The disclosures must state the dividend rate and the annual percentage yield (APY), which is the yearly return that includes the effect of compounding. They must also explain the balance computation method (for example, a daily balance method), the frequency of compounding and crediting, and any minimum balance or other condition needed to earn the stated rate or APY. Under NCUA Part 707, the credit union must give you the account disclosures for a new savings account before the account is opened. That way you can review the terms, fees, and rates before you are committed to the account. If you open an account over the phone, the rules allow the disclosures to be provided as soon as reasonably practicable after the account is opened, as long as you were told that you can close the account without penalty if you don't accept the terms. If you haven't received your disclosures and the account is already open, you can ask the credit union to send them to you.

Send the notice to the address the credit union has designated for billing error notices, not necessarily the address for payments. The notice should include your name and account number, the amount and date of the error, and why you believe it is a mistake. The card issuer must mail or deliver a written acknowledgment of your billing error notice within 30 days after it receives the notice. The only exception is if the issuer has already corrected the billing error within that 30-day period, in which case a written acknowledgment is not required. Because you have already sent a notice, a representative should confirm that it was received and is being tracked.

Under Regulation Z, once the card issuer receives your written billing error notice, it has up to two complete billing cycles to investigate, but no later than 90 days after it receives the notice. Within that time, it must either correct the error and credit your account, or send you a written explanation of why it believes the bill was correct. The clock runs from when the issuer receives your written notice, so the date it was received matters. Because you have an open dispute, a representative should confirm the date the notice was received and track the deadline.

You must notify the credit union at least three business days before the scheduled date of the automatic payment if you want it stopped. You can give that notice either by phone or in writing. If you give notice by phone, the credit union may require written confirmation within 14 days, and an oral stop order stops being binding after 14 days if that confirmation is not provided.

Whether you must follow up in writing depends on whether the credit union requires it. The credit union may require written confirmation of a stop-payment order within 14 days of an oral notification. You may want to ask the credit union whether it requires written confirmation for your stop-payment request.
